title: Europe's Hand-Copied Books
summary: For about a thousand years, every book in Europe was written out by hand with a feather pen. Monks painted pages with gold and bright blue, and one book could take months or even years to finish. By the 1400s so many people wanted books that the scribes simply could not keep up.

sections.heading: A Room Full of Scratching Quills
paragraphs: Imagine walking into a stone room in a monastery about 1,200 years ago. It is quiet except for a soft scratch, scratch, scratch. Along the walls, men in plain robes sit at slanted desks, each bent over a sheet of creamy animal skin. Each holds a feather pen in one hand and a small knife in the other. Some squint in the grey light from narrow windows, because candles were a fire risk near precious books. This room is a scriptorium, which simply means a place for writing. For most of the Middle Ages, rooms like this one were where Europe's books were born.

In Part 6 we saw Bi Sheng in China and the printers of Korea arranging movable type. Europe, at the very same time, had no printing of text at all. If you wanted a book, somebody had to copy it, letter by letter, from another book. That is what the word manuscript means: written by hand, from the Latin manus (hand) and scriptus (written).

Why monasteries? After the Western Roman Empire broke apart in the 400s, many of the old Roman schools and libraries faded away. Christian monasteries became some of the steadiest places of learning. Many followed the Rule of Saint Benedict, written in Italy in the 500s, which set aside hours each day for reading. Monks needed books for prayer, for church services and for study, so copying became part of holy work. A monk who copied a Bible was believed to be doing something good for his soul, and some scribes wrote little prayers at the end asking readers to remember them.

Monks did not only copy religious books. They also copied grammar books, histories, medical texts and works by Roman writers such as Virgil and Cicero. A great many ancient Latin texts that we can still read today survived only because medieval scribes kept copying them, generation after generation. Without those patient copyists, huge pieces of ancient knowledge would simply have vanished.

Let us look at a scribe's tools. His pen was a quill, made from a large flight feather, often from a goose. The feather was hardened, and the tip was cut with a penknife into a sharp, slanted nib. The nib wore down quickly, so the scribe kept his knife close by to reshape it. The same knife scraped away mistakes from the surface of the skin, and it also held the page flat while he wrote. Museums even have pictures of scribes with a quill in the right hand and a knife in the left, ready for action.

The ink was usually iron-gall ink. To make it, people collected oak galls, which are hard, round lumps that grow on oak trees when tiny wasps lay their eggs inside. The galls were crushed and soaked to release a chemical called tannic acid. Mixed with a compound of iron, the liquid turned a deep black. A sticky tree sap called gum arabic thickened it so it flowed nicely from the pen. Iron-gall ink soaks into the skin and becomes part of it, which is one reason so many medieval words are still crisp and dark today.

Before writing a single word, the scribe prepared the page. He pricked tiny holes down the edges with a sharp point, then drew faint guide lines between them using a ruler and a hard point or a lead stylus. These lines kept the writing straight and the columns tidy. If you look closely at old manuscripts, you can often still see those little pinpricks and ghostly ruled lines.

And the writing surface? Not paper, for most of this period. It was parchment, made from the skins of calves, sheep or goats. Skins were soaked in lime, scraped clean of hair and flesh, stretched tight on a frame, and dried. Very fine calfskin is called vellum. Parchment was tough and smooth, but it was costly, because each animal gave only a few large sheets. Little flaws in the skin sometimes stretched into holes, and careful scribes simply wrote around them.

sections.heading: Gold, Blue and Dragons: Illuminated Manuscripts
paragraphs: Some manuscripts were plain, made for everyday study. Others were works of art so dazzling that they are among the most treasured objects on Earth. These are called illuminated manuscripts. To illuminate means to light up, and that is exactly what gold and silver did when candlelight flickered across the page.

Making an illuminated page was teamwork. Usually the scribe wrote the text first, leaving blank spaces for pictures and big decorated first letters, called initials. Then an illuminator, sometimes a different person entirely, filled in the spaces. To add gold, the artist first painted a raised cushion of a chalky, glue-like paste called gesso. When it was just slightly sticky, he laid on a sheet of gold leaf so thin that a breath could blow it away. Then he rubbed it hard with a polished stone or even a dog's tooth until it gleamed like real metal, because it was real metal.

Colors came from all over nature. Blue could come from woad, a plant grown in Europe. A soft pink could come from madder roots. Green could come from verdigris, the greenish crust that forms on copper. Red often came from red lead, and a brilliant yellow came from orpiment, a mineral that contains arsenic, so painters had to be careful. The most precious blue of all was ultramarine, ground from the stone lapis lazuli, which came mainly from mines in what is now northern Afghanistan, thousands of kilometers away. Ultramarine could cost more than gold, so only the richest patrons could afford pages glowing with it.

Pigments were ground into powder and mixed with a binder such as egg white or gum so they would stick to the page. An artist might have small shells or pots of each color on the desk, and would build up a picture in thin layers. The result could be scenes from the Bible, portraits of saints, tiny animals climbing up the margins, or knights fighting snails. Yes, snails. Medieval artists loved silly and surprising little pictures in the margins, and historians still argue about what some of them mean.

The most famous illuminated manuscript of all may be the Book of Kells. It contains the four Gospels of the Bible in Latin, and it was made around the year 800. Most scholars think it was begun at the monastery on Iona, a small island off the west coast of Scotland, and it may have been finished at Kells in Ireland. After a Viking raid on Iona in 806, many monks moved to a new monastery at Kells, which is how the book got its name. Some scholars have suggested other places, such as northern England, so its exact birthplace is still debated.

The Book of Kells has about 340 leaves, called folios, of calfskin vellum, and each page today measures about 33 by 25.5 centimeters. Experts think about four main scribes copied the text and about three artists painted the great decorated pages. Its patterns are astonishing: spirals inside spirals, knots that twist without ever ending, and tiny cats, mice, birds and lions hidden among the letters. On its most famous page, the first letters of Christ's name in Greek, which look like the letters X and P, explode into a whirlwind of decoration.

Scientists at Trinity College Dublin, where the book is kept, have studied its colors with modern instruments. They found that its blue probably came from indigo or woad, not lapis lazuli as people once believed. That is a good reminder that even famous facts can change when scientists look more closely.

Interestingly, the Book of Kells contains quite a lot of copying mistakes. Experts think it was made mainly for show, to be displayed on the altar on special days like Easter, rather than read aloud every day. It was such a treasure that in about 1006, as old Irish records called the Annals of Ulster report, it was stolen for its jeweled cover. The book was found later, but its precious cover was gone forever. Today the Book of Kells is bound in four volumes, two are usually on display, and over half a million visitors a year come to see it in Dublin.

sections.heading: Months of Work for a Single Book
paragraphs: How long did it take to copy a book by hand? It depended on the book, the scribe and how fancy it was. A short schoolbook might take a skilled copyist a few weeks. A complete Bible, which is very long, could keep a scribe busy for many months, and a lavishly illuminated Bible could take a team years. Scribes worked only in daylight, often stopped for prayers and church services, and in winter cold could stiffen their fingers.

Copying was hard on the body, too. Scribes sometimes left complaints in the margins or at the end of a book. One old manuscript, kept today in Paris, contains a line that is often translated as 'Three fingers write, the whole body suffers.' Others grumbled about bad ink, thin parchment, the cold, or simply being hungry. Reading these notes, you can almost hear a tired scribe sighing over his desk.

At the end of a book, a scribe sometimes wrote a colophon, a short note saying who copied it, where, and for whom. For example, an Old English copy of the Gospel of Matthew from the early 1000s has a note in Latin from a scribe named Aelfric, who says he wrote it at Bath for a man named Brihtwold. Notes like this are precious to historians, because most medieval book-makers never wrote their names at all.

Books were built from bundles called quires. A scribe or workshop took several large sheets of parchment, folded them in half, and nested them together, a bit like a stack of folded birthday cards tucked inside each other. Each quire might be written by a different scribe working at the same time, which sped things up. When all the quires were done, a binder sewed them together onto strong cords or leather straps and attached them to wooden boards, which were often covered in leather. Some covers on special books were decorated with metal, carved ivory or jewels.

Now think about cost. The parchment alone for a big book could need the skins of many animals. Then there were the scribe's wages or keep, the ink, the colors, the gold, and the binding. A large, decorated book might cost as much as a house or a farm. Ordinary books were cheaper, but still far beyond what most working people could afford. Books were so valuable that many libraries chained them to the desks or shelves so that nobody could walk off with them.

Hand-copying had another problem: errors. Every time a text was copied, the scribe might skip a line, misread a word or repeat a phrase. The next scribe copied the mistakes and added new ones. After many generations, different copies of the same book could disagree in hundreds of small places. Scholars had to compare copies and guess which reading was right. This is one reason why, as we will see in later parts, printing thousands of identical copies was such a big deal for learning and science.

sections.heading: Students, Stationers and Books for Rent
paragraphs: Around the year 1100 and after, something new appeared in Europe: the university. Bologna in Italy is usually counted as the oldest, with roots in the late 1000s, and it became famous for law. Paris grew into a great center for theology and philosophy around 1200, and Oxford in England was teaching students by the late 1100s. Soon there were universities in Cambridge, Padua, Salamanca, Prague and many other cities.

Universities changed the book world. Monks had copied books mostly for their own monasteries. Now thousands of students and teachers in a single city all needed the same textbooks at the same time: law books, works of the Greek thinker Aristotle in Latin translation, commentaries on the Bible, and medical texts. One monk copying one book for many months could never keep up with that.

So the universities invented a clever system. It was called the pecia system, from a Latin word meaning a piece. It had grown up in Italian university towns by the early 1200s, and the University of Paris turned it into a carefully regulated procedure in the second half of the 1200s. Here is how it worked. Teachers checked a text to make sure it was correct. A bookseller, called a stationer, then had an official master copy made, called the exemplar. Instead of binding the exemplar as one book, the stationer kept it as loose pieces, each usually four folios long.

Before any renting began, officials from the university inspected the exemplar and set the price a student would pay to borrow each piece. A student, or a scribe the student paid, would rent piece number one, copy it, return it, and rent piece number two. Meanwhile someone else could be copying piece number five, and someone else piece number twelve. Because many people could copy different parts of the same book at once, new copies were made much faster than if one scribe had to wait for a whole book. It was a bit like a library that lends out one chapter at a time so that the whole class can share.

Why the strict rules? The university wanted students to study accurate texts, at fair prices. Officials checked exemplars from time to time for errors. Copies made from pecia exemplars have been identified from Paris and several Italian university towns, and sometimes you can still see little notes in the margins marking where one piece ended and the next began.

Universities also helped create a new kind of worker: the professional scribe who was not a monk. These lay scribes, meaning people who were not members of the clergy, copied books for pay. Stationers and booksellers, called librarii in Latin, bought and sold new and secondhand books, and the universities regulated them. In Paris, booksellers had to swear oaths and post money as a guarantee of good behavior. By the 1300s and 1400s, cities like Paris, Bruges and Florence had busy book workshops where scribes, illuminators and binders worked for paying customers, much like small businesses today.

The handwriting changed too. Many university books and later manuscripts were written in a compact, upright style historians call Gothic script, with tall, narrow letters packed tightly together. Narrow letters meant more words fit on each expensive page. To save even more space and time, scribes used lots of abbreviations, little marks and shortened words that readers learned to understand. When Gutenberg designed his first types, as we will see in Part 9, he copied this Gothic handwriting, abbreviations and all, so his printed pages would look like the best manuscripts.

sections.heading: Merchants, Prayer Books and a Growing Hunger to Read
paragraphs: You may have heard that people in the Middle Ages could not read and did not care about learning. That is a myth. It is true that most farmers and laborers could not read, and books were rare and costly. But the Middle Ages also produced universities, great poets, scientists, lawyers and libraries, and over time more and more people learned to read.

By the 1300s and 1400s, towns across Europe were growing richer. Merchants in Italy, Flanders and Germany traded wool, cloth, spices and silver over long distances. To do business, they had to write letters, keep account books, sign contracts and check bills. Many merchant families sent their sons, and sometimes daughters, to schools where they learned reading, writing and arithmetic. Some Italian cities had schools that taught calculation using the new Hindu-Arabic numerals, the 0 to 9 digits we use today.

More reading also meant more writing in everyday languages, not just Latin. In Italy, Dante Alighieri wrote his great poem, the Divine Comedy, in Italian in the early 1300s. In England, Geoffrey Chaucer wrote the Canterbury Tales in English in the late 1300s. Townspeople wanted stories, histories, songs, and practical books about health, cooking, farming and travel, written in a language they actually spoke at home.

Paper made a big difference. As we saw in Part 4, paper mills had spread through Italy, Spain and then other parts of Europe during the 1300s. Paper was much cheaper than parchment, so a book written on paper cost less, and a merchant could buy reams of it for letters and accounts. Governments, courts and churches produced mountains of documents, from tax lists to legal records, and many of them were now on paper.

The best-selling book of the late Middle Ages was not a novel or a science book. It was the book of hours, a personal prayer book for ordinary people who were not monks or priests. It contained a calendar of saints' days and short prayers to be said at different hours of the day, imitating the services monks sang in monasteries. Historians often call it a medieval bestseller: from roughly the 1300s to the mid-1500s, books of hours were made in enormous numbers, and today they are the most common kind of illuminated manuscript to survive, with tens of thousands still in existence.

Books of hours came in every price range. Kings and dukes ordered breathtaking ones painted by top artists, like the famous Very Rich Hours of the Duke of Berry, begun in the early 1400s. Merchant families bought simpler ones with just a few pictures. Many children even learned their letters by reading from the family book of hours. Workshops in Paris, Bruges and other cities turned them out in large numbers, sometimes making parts in advance and adding the owner's coat of arms or favorite saints at the end.

Even so, books were still scarce by modern standards. In about 1424, the common library of the University of Cambridge listed only 122 volumes, and more than half of them were about theology and religion. By 1473 it had grown to about 330 volumes. Before about 1450, even a large and important library in Europe might hold only a few hundred books.

All of this added up to a growing problem. More readers, more schools, more universities, more merchants, more cheap paper, but still only one way to make a copy of a book: by hand. Demand was racing ahead of supply.

sections.heading: Pictures Carved in Wood
paragraphs: Long before Europeans printed books with type, they began printing pictures. Once paper became common in Europe, around 1400, craftspeople began making woodcuts. A woodcut is made the same basic way as the Chinese woodblocks we met in Part 5. The artist draws a picture on a smooth plank of wood, then cuts away everything except the lines, leaving them standing up. The raised lines are inked, paper is pressed on top, and the picture appears, reversed like a mirror image.

Many of the earliest European woodcuts were religious pictures of saints, Jesus or the Virgin Mary. They were cheap enough for ordinary people to buy, perhaps at a pilgrimage site or a church festival. People pasted them on walls, inside chests, or into their prayer books. Many were colored in by hand afterwards with quick strokes of red, green and yellow. Because they were cheap and stuck up on walls, most were simply worn out and thrown away, so only a small number survive.

One of the most famous is a woodcut of Saint Christopher carrying the child Jesus across a river, with a little hermit holding a lantern, a man on a mule, and even a rabbit tucked into the scene. It bears the date 1423 written in Latin, and it was discovered in 1769, pasted inside the binding of a manuscript from the monastery library of Buxheim in southern Germany. Only one copy printed from this block survives, and it is kept at the John Rylands Library in Manchester, England.

For a long time this Saint Christopher was called the earliest dated European print. But here is a nice piece of detective work: a recent study pointed out that the style of the picture looks more like the 1440s and 1450s, and a watermark in its paper matches papers used around 1428 to 1435. So the 1423 date may not be when it was printed. It might mark something else, such as a religious occasion. The study concluded that it was probably printed in the mid-to-late 1430s.

Woodcuts were also used for playing cards. Card games had arrived in Europe in the late 1300s, and they became hugely popular. Hand-painted cards were expensive, but cards printed from woodblocks and colored with stencils could be made quickly and cheaply. In the 1400s there were card-makers in towns like Ulm and Nuremberg in Germany. Cards may have been one of the first printed products that ordinary Europeans used every day.

Then came block books. A block book is a short book in which each page, pictures and words together, was carved on a single block of wood, just like a Chinese woodblock page. Most European block books date from about the 1450s to the 1470s, so they appeared around the same time as early printing with metal type, not long before it as people once thought. They were made mainly in Germany and the Netherlands.

Popular block books included the Biblia pauperum, a picture Bible showing scenes from the life of Jesus side by side with matching stories from the Old Testament; the Ars moriendi, or Art of Dying, which gave advice on facing death with a peaceful heart; and illustrated versions of the Apocalypse, the last book of the Bible. They were heavy on pictures and light on words, because carving lots of tiny letters into wood was slow and fiddly. If you made one mistake while carving a letter, you could not easily fix it, so cutting a whole page of text into one block was risky work.

Block books show us something important. Europeans already knew how to print images on paper. What they did not yet have was a fast, flexible way to print large amounts of text. For that, they would need not a single carved block for each page, but thousands of tiny, separate letters that could be used again and again.

sections.heading: A Continent Ready for Something New
paragraphs: Let us step back and look at Europe around 1440. There are dozens of universities full of students who need textbooks. There are rich merchants who keep accounts and like to read. There are schools teaching children Latin grammar from little books. There are millions of Christians who want prayer books, and a church that needs huge numbers of service books, Bibles and official documents. There are lawyers, doctors, preachers and city clerks who all need texts.

On the supply side, there is cheap paper from mills in Italy, France and Germany. There are woodcut makers who know how to press ink onto paper. There are goldsmiths and metalworkers who are experts at casting small, precise objects and stamping metal with punches, like the punches used to make coins. There are wine presses and paper presses with big wooden screws, standing in vineyards and paper mills. All the pieces of a new invention are lying around, waiting for someone to put them together in the right way.

It is worth remembering what medieval scribes achieved. For roughly a thousand years they kept the knowledge of ancient Rome and Greece alive, created new learning, and produced some of the most beautiful objects ever made. Many people at the time thought hand-written books were finer than printed ones, and scribes kept working for decades after printing arrived.

But the numbers were against the scribes. A single scribe might finish a few books a year. Europe now wanted thousands. The world needed a way to copy words not one at a time, but hundreds at a time, all exactly the same.
In the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith with big debts and a bigger idea was getting ready to change all of this.

deepDive: How many books were there in medieval Europe, and how many people could read them? Historians cannot count every lost manuscript, so they work from what survives, from library catalogues and from tax and court records. Economic historians have tried to estimate total manuscript production century by century, and their work suggests output rose steeply from the 1100s onward, especially after universities appeared and paper became common. These estimates come with large error bars, because many manuscripts were destroyed by fire, war, damp, reuse as binding scraps or simple neglect. Literacy is just as tricky to measure. Being able to read was not the same as being able to write, and many people could read a little in their own language without knowing Latin. Some historians use signatures on documents as a rough guide, while others point to the huge market for books of hours as evidence that reading spread well beyond monks and nobles, including to many women. The pecia system is a good example of medieval problem-solving: by splitting an approved exemplar into rentable pieces, universities increased copying speed and controlled accuracy and price, a kind of quality control centuries before factories. Dating early prints is a science of its own. Experts compare artistic style, look at paper watermarks (each paper mill's mould left a distinctive wire design), and study how a woodblock cracked or wore down between impressions. The famous Saint Christopher dated 1423 shows why dates printed on an object do not always tell you when it was made; watermark evidence now points to the 1430s. Finally, historians stress that print did not replace manuscripts overnight. Scribes, illuminators and stationers continued working into the 1500s, often decorating printed books by hand; one of the first great printers, Peter Schoeffer, had himself been a scribe. Many early printers were former scribes who brought their skills with them.
funFact: Scientists at Trinity College Dublin found that the blue in the Book of Kells probably came from indigo or woad plants, not from the expensive gemstone lapis lazuli that people had believed for many years.
